reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Characterised by numerous tiny, pinpoint (around 1 mm), flat-topped, shiny papules that are skin-coloured or hypopigmented
Papules are typically grouped in clusters on the flexor forearms, genitalia (often the penile shaft), abdomen, and chest
The Koebner phenomenon is common, with lesions appearing in a line along sites of scratching or trauma
Predominantly affects children and young adults and is usually asymptomatic
Considered by some to be a variant or close relative of lichen planus, though most regard it as a distinct entity
Nail changes (ridging, pitting) and, uncommonly, palmoplantar or generalised forms may occur
Histology is characteristic, showing a well-circumscribed lymphohistiocytic infiltrate embraced by elongated rete ridges in a ball-and-claw configuration
Usually self-limiting; treatment (topical corticosteroids, occasionally phototherapy) is reserved for symptomatic or cosmetically troublesome disease
reference.pathophysiology: Lichen nitidus is an inflammatory dermatosis in which a focal, cell-mediated response involving T-lymphocytes and histiocytes targets the epidermis, producing the characteristic sharply circumscribed papular infiltrate. The precise trigger is unknown, and although it shares a lichenoid tissue reaction with lichen planus, the two are usually considered separate conditions. The dense but tiny granulomatous focus, held between elongated rete ridges, corresponds to the minute shiny papule seen clinically, and the tendency to Koebnerise reflects an antigen-independent response to local trauma.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy demonstrating the characteristic ball-and-claw granulomatous focus in the papillary dermis
Dermoscopy to appreciate the uniform, shiny, discrete papules
Assessment for the Koebner phenomenon along scratch lines as a diagnostic clue
Nail examination where nail dystrophy is suspected
Review for features of lichen planus overlap (oral, nail, and scalp involvement)
Evaluation for tuberculosis where lichen scrofulosorum is a serious consideration
redFlags: Widespread or generalised eruption that fails to remit and warrants reassessment
Features suggesting lichen scrofulosorum, prompting evaluation for underlying tuberculosis
Nail dystrophy or mucosal change suggesting overlap with lichen planus
reference.prognosis: Benign, typically resolving spontaneously over months to a few years without scarring, although the course can occasionally be more protracted.
pitfalls: Confusing the pinpoint papules with keratosis pilaris or plane warts
Overlooking the Koebner phenomenon as a helpful diagnostic feature
Failing to distinguish it from lichen scrofulosorum, which mandates a tuberculosis workup
